doc.title: Ellis Marsalis — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Club owners, the academy and education
title: Graduation rates and funding politicians
summary: He criticizes funding tied to graduation rates, citing Bill Gates and Brian Williams.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Life philosophy: faith, karma and how to live

blocks.x: So consequently, the open-ended situation – when I say open-ended, there was a young lady that I heard – I didn’t get to know her that well – went to Virginia Commonwealth. By the time I got to Virginia Commonwealth, she was doing a senior recital. She was a vocalist. I think that was her main thing, but I don’t know. Anyway, she had to sing the usual three languages, Italian, French, German. She had also been studying in the jazz studies division with the band teacher, arranging. She arranged two or three pieces for jazz band. What – the overall program that she did crossed all them lines. I asked about her. She went on and off at that school for eight years. To me, that’s conviction. I don’t know if I could do that. But the point is that I don’t know in a lot of cases that one needs to do that. The biggest mistake that politicians make – and they make a lot – is that the ones that are determining the funding that goes into the – especially into the state universities – have used as a criteria, how many people graduate? What makes that a fallacy is this: Bill

Gates ain’t finished nothing. I just found out lately. You know the cat on the NBC News, Brian Williams? He went to three different junior colleges. Didn’t finish none of that. The point here is this: if there was a formula in which the university – and they could do it easily – can say, okay, between 2010 and 2012, we enrolled X amount of students. During that same period of time, there were X amount of students who dropped out. The following two years, there was a return of a certain percentage of the students who had dropped out. So eventually, you get a picture of, let’s see, the effectiveness of the institution was that it was here for the students to come and go, come and go, come and go. So rather than say, okay – because from what I understand, 50% of all of them schools lose – they lose about 50% of the students. That’s what I understand. I don’t know. But when you get to – if you start out with a thousand, and four years later, 400 graduate, so the legislature penalizes them? Because 1,000 didn’t graduate?
Sounds like they’re back to the bottom line. They’re looking at it . . . .

They have never left it. The problem is that the people who put them in office, they don’t understand any of the process anyway. So the politicians will come up with any process and say, okay, let’s see, they’ll buy into this. Run it out there. They say, oh, they’ll do that? Okay. Then they’ll do that. How many times have you heard the term “welfare reform”? Go look at the pie. You know that pie?
